analogy.p: A 1D array is a row of **identical lockers** with one name for the whole row, say scores, and each locker has a number that **starts at 0**. You ask for locker number 2 by writing scores[2], and you can replace what is inside without touching the others. The number of lockers is fixed when the row is built. A 2D array is a **car park with rows and bays**: to find a car you need the row number and the bay number, written grid[row,column], and walking round it row by row is like a nested loop. The analogy breaks down because real lockers can be added or removed, whereas a static array in programming has a fixed size and every locker must hold the same type of data.
analogy.t: A row of numbered lockers (and a car park)

bullets: An array holds **many values under one identifier** (name), such as scores or names.
All the elements are the **same data type**: an array of integers, or an array of strings, not a mixture.
The **size is fixed** when the array is declared; a **static** array cannot grow or shrink while the program runs.
Each element is accessed with its **index** in square brackets, e.g. scores[2].
A **one-dimensional (1D)** array is like a single row of boxes; a **two-dimensional (2D)** array is like a table with rows and columns.
Link to other topics: variables and data types (2.2), loops (2.2), file handling (2.2), searching and sorting algorithms (2.1).
core.p: An **array** is a **data structure** that stores a **fixed number of items under one name**, with every item of the **same data type**. Instead of creating five separate variables score1, score2, score3, score4 and score5, you create one array called scores and refer to each item by its **position**. Each item is called an **element** and its position number is its **index**. The J277 specification describes arrays as **fixed-length static structures** that can be **one-dimensional** (a list) or **two-dimensional** (a table of rows and columns). Arrays are one of the main tools for handling lots of related data in a program.

bullets: **Fewer variables**: one array replaces many separate variables, which keeps the program tidy.
Loops can process every element using a counter as the index, so **the code stays the same however many values** there are.
Easy to apply the same operation to all data: total, average, find the highest, count how many are above a limit.
Data can be **searched** and **sorted** because items are held in numbered positions.
Arrays can be filled from a **file** or from user input in a loop and written back out later.
Disadvantage: the size is fixed, so you must know in advance how many items there will be, and all items must be the same type.
core.p: Arrays make programs shorter, clearer and easier to change. With separate variables you would need a separate line of code for each value and the program could not cope with more data without being rewritten. With an array a **loop** can step through every element using the index as a counter, so the same few lines handle 5 or 500 values. Arrays also keep related data together, which makes totals, averages, searching and sorting much simpler to write. This is the key idea behind most array questions: the index and the loop counter work together.

bullets: Reference language: **array names[6]** declares an array called names with six elements.
The number in brackets is the **number of elements**, so array scores[5] has indexes 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.
Choose a meaningful **identifier** (scores, names, prices) so the purpose is clear.
Declaring the array does not give the elements useful values; assign values or read them in a loop.
Python equivalent: **scores = [0] * 5** creates five zeros; Python lists are more flexible, but exam questions on arrays treat them as fixed size.
If a question gives the size as a constant (for example 30 students) use the correct number in the declaration and in the loop limits.
core.p: Before an array can be used it must be **declared**, which tells the computer its name and how many elements to reserve. In the OCR reference language this is written array scores[5], which creates an array called scores with room for five elements. The number in the brackets is the **size** (the number of elements), not the last index. A declared array is usually empty or holds default values until you assign values to its elements. In Python the same idea is a **list**, for example scores = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0], although Python lists can change size.

bullets: **First element is at index 0**: scores[0].
**Last element = size - 1**: in array scores[5] the last is scores[4].
The array scores[5] has **5 elements** but the highest valid index is **4**.
Using an index that does not exist (e.g. scores[5], scores[-1] in the reference language) causes an **index out of range error**.
A loop that visits every element goes from **0 to size - 1**: for i = 0 to 4 for a size 5 array.
Write the indexes above each box when you trace; it avoids the 'off by one' mistake (using 1 to 5 instead of 0 to 4).
core.p: The **index** is the position of an element, and in OCR J277 and in Python the **first index is 0**. This means an array with 5 elements has indexes 0 to 4: the **last index is always the size minus one**. Mixing up the number of elements with the last index is the most common array error. Trying to use an index outside the valid range, for example scores[5] in an array of size 5, is an **out of range (index) error**, and the program will stop. When tracing, always write the index numbers above or below the array so you can see exactly which box is used.

bullets: Assign: **scores[0] = 12** (store 12 in the first element).
Read/output: **print(scores[2])** displays the value stored at index 2.
Overwrite: **scores[2] = scores[2] + 5** changes only element 2; the other elements stay the same.
The index can be a **variable**: scores[i], so one line of code can access any element as i changes.
Swap two elements with a temporary variable: temp = scores[0]; scores[0] = scores[1]; scores[1] = temp.
To fill an array from the user: for i = 0 to 4, then scores[i] = input("Enter score"), then next i (convert with int() if numbers are needed).
core.p: To **store** a value you assign to an element using its index: scores[0] = 12 puts 12 into the first box. To **read** a value you use the same notation on the right of an assignment or inside a statement: print(scores[2]) outputs the third element, and total = total + scores[i] adds the element at index i. Assigning to an element **overwrites** the old value; no other elements change. The index can be a number, a variable such as i, or an expression such as i + 1, which is what lets loops work through the array.

bullets: Pattern: **for i = 0 to 4**, **print(scores[i])**, **next i** displays all five elements.
The loop counter **i** is used as the index, so it takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 in turn.
The limits must be **0 to size - 1**; to 5 would cause an error for a size 5 array.
Use a for loop because the number of elements is known; a while loop is for when the number of repeats is not known.
Inside the loop you can **read** an element (output, add) or **change** it (scores[i] = scores[i] + 1).
Python equivalent: for i in range(5): print(scores[i]) (range(5) gives 0 to 4) or simply for item in scores.
core.h: Using a for loop to traverse an array
core.p: **Traversing** an array means visiting every element in turn. Because the size is fixed and known, a **for loop** (count-controlled iteration) is the natural choice. The loop variable i starts at 0 and finishes at the last index (size - 1), and inside the loop scores[i] is the element currently being processed. This pattern is the basis of totalling, averaging, counting, finding the largest and searching. When writing it, make sure the loop limits match the array size exactly, otherwise you will either miss an element or cause an out of range error.

bullets: **Total**: total = 0; for i = 0 to 4; total = total + scores[i]; next i. Remember to set total to 0 **before** the loop.
**Average**: total / size (for 5 elements, divide by 5); do the division **after** the loop.
**Largest**: highest = scores[0]; then if scores[i] > highest then highest = scores[i] inside the loop. Smallest is the same with <.
**Count** how many are above a limit: count = 0; if scores[i] > 10 then count = count + 1.
**Linear search**: check each element in order; set found = True (and note i) when scores[i] == target; stop or finish the loop.
All of these can be combined with a file: read values from the file into the array, process them, write the result.
core.p: A small group of algorithms appear again and again. To find a **total** you set a variable to 0 before the loop and add each element inside the loop; the **average** is the total divided by the number of elements. To find the **largest** value you assume the first element is the largest, then compare every other element and replace the stored value if you find a bigger one. To **count** items you add 1 to a counter whenever a condition is true. To **search**, you compare each element with the target and record when it matches (a **linear search**). Each uses the for loop pattern and the index.

bullets: Two arrays, e.g. **names[5]** and **scores[5]**, linked by **having the same index**.
To find the score of a named person: search names for the name to get index i, then output scores[i].
Both arrays must be **kept in the same order**; changing the position of one without the other breaks the link.
They let you store **different data types** side by side (strings in one array, integers in the other), which a single array cannot.
Printing a table: for i = 0 to 4, then print(names[i] + " " + str(scores[i])).
Alternatives: a **2D array** (all one type) or a **record** (see records and SQL) for a group of fields.
core.p: Sometimes you need to store several pieces of information about the same things, such as a name and a score for each student. A **parallel array** approach uses **two (or more) separate 1D arrays** where **the same index refers to the same person or item**. If names[2] is Cy then scores[2] holds Cy's score. Arrays must be the same size and kept in step, so if you swap two scores in a sort you must swap the matching names too. Parallel arrays are an alternative to a 2D array (which must hold one data type) and to records.

bullets: Declare: **array grid[3,4]** gives 3 rows and 4 columns, which is 3 x 4 = **12 elements**.
Access: **grid[row,column]**: the **row index comes first**, then the column index.
Valid row indexes are 0 to 2 and valid column indexes are 0 to 3 for grid[3,4].
Assign: **grid[1,2] = 9** puts 9 in row 1, column 2 and changes only that cell.
Think of it as an array of arrays: each row is itself a 1D array.
Using a row or column number that is too large causes an **index out of range** error, just as in a 1D array.
core.p: A **two-dimensional (2D) array** stores data in a **table with rows and columns**, so each element needs **two indexes**: the row and the column. In the OCR reference language an array with 3 rows and 4 columns is declared array grid[3,4], and an element is written grid[row,column]. As with 1D arrays, both indexes start at 0. So grid[1,2] is in the **second row** and the **third column**. A 2D array is useful whenever the data naturally forms a grid, and all the elements are still the **same data type**.

bullets: Pattern: **for row = 0 to 2**, **for col = 0 to 3**, **print(grid[row,col])**, **next col**, **next row**.
The **outer loop** controls the rows; the **inner loop** controls the columns.
Total passes = rows x columns, here 3 x 4 = 12.
For a **row total**, keep the row fixed and loop over the columns only; for a **column total** keep the column fixed and loop over the rows.
To total the whole array put total = 0 before both loops and total = total + grid[row,col] in the inner loop.
Match each limit to the correct dimension; swapping them is a common source of out of range errors.
core.h: Traversing a 2D array with nested loops
core.p: To visit every element in a 2D array you need **two loops, one inside the other**, called **nested loops**. The **outer loop** steps through the rows and the **inner loop** steps through the columns of the current row. The inner loop runs all the way through for every pass of the outer loop, so the elements are visited **row by row**, left to right. For grid[3,4] the outer loop is for row = 0 to 2 and the inner loop is for col = 0 to 3, giving 12 passes of the inner statement. Inside, grid[row,col] is the current element.

bullets: **Game boards**: noughts and crosses uses grid[3,3] holding "X", "O" or "".
**Seating plan**: seats[10,8] where "Y" or "N" shows if a seat is booked; booking changes one cell.
**Timetable** or **results table**: row for each student or day, column for each subject or lesson.
**Image pixels**: each element stores a colour value for one pixel; the position in the grid is the pixel's position.
Searching a 2D array needs **nested loops**, comparing each cell with the target.
Choose a 2D array when all items are the same type; if rows hold different types, use parallel arrays or records.
core.p: 2D arrays represent any data that is laid out in a grid. In games they store a **board** (noughts and crosses, chess, a maze or a tile map), where each cell holds a piece or a number. They store a **seating plan** for a cinema or an exam hall with a value showing whether each seat is taken, a **timetable** with days and periods, **pixel values** of an image, or a **spreadsheet-like table** of results. The same techniques apply every time: nested loops to visit cells, and two indexes to read or update a particular cell, for example when a seat is booked.

bullets: **Array**: fixed length, one data type, accessed by index; best for a list of similar items.
**List (Python)**: can change size and hold mixed types; flexible but not the same as the fixed OCR array.
**Record**: a group of related **fields** about one thing; each field can have a different data type.
**2D array**: a table of one data type; **parallel arrays** are a way of storing different types by index.
A fixed-length array can **waste memory** if it is larger than needed, or run out of room if it is too small.
Link to other topics: records and SQL (2.2), data types (2.2), searching and sorting algorithms (2.1), file handling (2.2).
core.p: The J277 specification describes arrays as **static**: the size is fixed when they are created. Some languages, including Python, use **lists** that can grow and shrink while the program runs (dynamic structures), but exam questions based on the reference language assume a fixed size. A **record** groups different data types about one item (such as name, age and score), and is stored in a database as a row. Arrays are best when you have many values of the same type and need to loop through them by index. Knowing when to use each structure helps with design questions.

bullets: Read into array: i = 0; while NOT myFile.endOfFile(); names[i] = myFile.readLine(); i = i + 1; endwhile; myFile.close().
Write from array: for i = 0 to 4; myFile.writeLine(names[i]); next i; myFile.close().
The array must be **large enough** for all the lines in the file, or an index out of range error occurs.
**Boundary testing**: test the first element (index 0) and the last element (size - 1) and an index just outside the range.
Use a **trace table** with columns for i and each array element to check your algorithm before running it.
Link to other topics: file handling (2.2), validation (2.3), testing (2.3), sorting and searching (2.1).
core.h: Arrays and files together, and testing
core.p: Arrays are often filled from a file at the start of a program and written back at the end. To read a file into an array you use a counter as the index: each readLine is stored in the next element, and the counter goes up by 1. To save an array you loop through it and writeLine each element. Good programmers also **test** array code using normal, boundary and erroneous data, including arrays with one element and the **first and last index**, because the most common faults happen at the ends of the array. Also check the loop limits against the size.

exam: **State/Identify** (1 mark): give the value of an element, e.g. 'grid[1,2] is 9'. Write the index numbers over the array first to avoid off-by-one errors.
**Describe an array** (2 marks): a data structure that holds a fixed number (1) of items of the same data type under one name, accessed by an index (1).
**Why use an array instead of separate variables** (2-3 marks): fewer variables/less code; can use a loop to process every element; easier to add more data.
**Write/complete code** (3-5 marks): declare with array name[size], correct loop limits (0 to size - 1), use name[i], initialise totals before the loop, output after the loop.
**Trace** (3-4 marks): draw a trace table with i and the array contents; update element values when the code assigns to them.
**2D arrays**: use the format array[row,column] and nested loops. Check which index is the row and which the column.
**Describe an algorithm** such as linear search (4 marks): start at the first element, compare each with the target, stop if found (report the position), otherwise report not found at the end.
**Spotting errors**: look for loop limits that go to the size instead of size - 1, missing initialisation, and use of the wrong index.
**Compare data structures** (4 marks): array = fixed size, one type; record = different types per item; list = dynamic. Give a reason for each.
Use clear identifiers (scores, names, grid) and indent loops; the longer programming questions award marks for good style as well as logic.

mistakes.r: The first element is at index 0; an array of size n has indexes 0 to n - 1.
mistakes.w: Saying the first element is at index 1.

mistakes.r: The last index is 4, so for i = 0 to 4; to 5 causes an index out of range error.
mistakes.w: Writing for i = 0 to 5 for an array declared array scores[5].

mistakes.r: The row index comes first, then the column index.
Initialise total (and counters) to 0 before the loop so the total starts correctly.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to set total = 0 before the loop.

mistakes.r: Divide the total by the number of elements, after the loop has finished.
mistakes.w: Dividing by the wrong number when finding an average.

mistakes.r: An array holds one data type; use parallel arrays or a record for mixed data.
mistakes.w: Putting different data types in one array.

mistakes.r: A (static) array has a fixed size set when it is declared.
mistakes.w: Saying an array can grow when more items are added.

mistakes.r: Use nested loops: the outer loop for rows and the inner loop for columns.
mistakes.w: Using a single loop to traverse a 2D array.

mistakes.r: Start with the first element, best = scores[0], then compare the rest.
mistakes.w: Starting best = 0 when finding the largest in data that could be negative.

summary: OCR J277 spec section 2.2 expects you to use one- and two-dimensional arrays as fixed-length (static) structures: declare them, read and change elements by index, and traverse them with for loops and nested loops. It matters because arrays underpin totals, searches, tables and game boards, and index and loop questions appear in every Paper 2.

terms.d: A data structure that stores a fixed number of elements of the same data type under one identifier.
A single item stored in an array.
The number that gives the position of an element in an array; the first index is 0.
An array with one index; a simple list of elements in a single row.
An array with two indexes, row and column, storing data in a table.
A data structure whose size is fixed when it is created and cannot change while the program runs.
To state the name and size of an array so that the computer reserves space for it, e.g. array scores[5].
To visit every element of an array in turn, usually with a loop.
A loop placed inside another loop; used to traverse a 2D array.
The error caused by using an index that does not exist in the array.
Two or more arrays in which the same index refers to related data about the same item.
An algorithm that checks each element in order until the target is found or the end is reached.
A horizontal set of elements in a 2D array; the first index.
A vertical set of elements in a 2D array; the second index.
The name given to a variable, array or other item in a program.
The kind of data stored, such as integer, real, Boolean, character or string.

steps: (a) Index 3 is the fourth element: 12 (0), 8 (1), 15 (2), 6 (3), 10 (4), so scores[3] = 6.
Set total = 0 before the loop (1 mark).
for i = 0 to 4 with total = total + scores[i] inside, then next i (2 marks).
Average = total / 5 after the loop, then print (1 mark).

worked.q: The 2D array grid[3,4] is: row 0 = 3, 5, 2, 8; row 1 = 7, 1, 9, 4; row 2 = 6, 0, 5, 2. (a) State grid[1,2] and grid[2,3]. (b) Write code to output the total of row 1. [5 marks]
steps: (a) The row is given first: row 1 is 7, 1, 9, 4, and column 2 is the third item, so grid[1,2] = 9.
Row 2 is 6, 0, 5, 2 and column 3 is the fourth item, so grid[2,3] = 2.
(b) Set total = 0, then loop the columns only: for col = 0 to 3, with row fixed at 1.
Inside the loop: total = total + grid[1,col]; after the loop print(total).

worked.ans: One array, marks[30], replaces 30 separate variables, which makes the program shorter and easier to maintain. A for loop can use the index to process each mark (for example to total them) with the same few lines of code, and the marks can be searched or sorted easily because each is stored at a numbered position.
worked.q: Explain two advantages of using an array rather than separate variables to store 30 test marks. [3 marks]
steps: Advantage 1: only one identifier is needed instead of 30, so the program is shorter and easier to read (1 mark).
Advantage 2: a loop can use the index to process every mark, e.g. totalling them, so the same code works for any number of marks (1 mark).
Extra point: marks can easily be searched or sorted because they are stored in numbered positions (1 mark).
